**Los Angeles – Current Air‑Quality Overview**

> *Note:* As a text‑based AI I don’t have real‑time internet connectivity, so I cannot pull today’s exact numbers from the field. Below you’ll find everything you need to know to get up‑to‑date information yourself—and what those figures typically mean for your day‑to‑day life.

---

### How to Check Today’s Air Quality Index (AQI)

| Source | What It Offers | Quick Access |
|--------|-----------------|--------------|
| **EPA AirNow** | Official U.S. government site providing hourly AQI readings for all monitoring stations across California. Includes pollutant breakdowns (PM₂.₅, PM₁₀, Ozone, CO, NO₂). | <https://www.airnow.gov/> → “Find Your Local Station” → Enter ZIP code (e.g., 90001–90099 for L.A.) |
| **AirVisual / IQAir** | Global database with near‑real‑time AQI, forecast, and historical trends. Mobile app & web dashboard. | <https://iqair.com/usa/california/la-air-quality> |
| **BreezoMeter** | Real‑time pollution map + personalized alerts via mobile push notifications. | <https://breezometer.com/maps/#map=la> |
| **Local News Outlets** | Many newspapers/cable networks publish daily “weather & smog” segments. Example: KABC-TV, KTLA. | Search “L.A. smog report” on their websites. |

#### Step‑by‑Step:

1. **Open one of the links above** (or search “Los Angeles AQI”).
2. **Enter your ZIP code or city name** if prompted.
3. Look at the displayed **AQI value**:
   - 0–50 Good  
   - 51–100 Moderate  
   - 101–150 Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups  
   - 151–200 Unhealthy  
   - 201–300 Very Unhealthy  
   - 301+ Hazardous  

4. If you’re interested in specific pollutants, click the detailed view—most platforms show percentages for each component.

---

### Typical Daily Patterns in Los Angeles

| Time of Day | Common Pollutants | Why It Happens |
|-------------|-------------------|---------------|
| Early morning (5–9 AM) | High ozone levels due to overnight temperature inversions | Sunlight starts breaking down nitrogen oxides into ozone |
| Mid‑morning (10 AM–12 NOON) | Peak ozone | Solar radiation peaks |
| Afternoon (1–5 PM) | Elevated particulate matter (especially during wildfire season) | Dust, vehicle emissions, wildfires |
| Evening/night | Lower overall AQI, though sometimes high PM₂.₅ from lingering smoke | Cooler temperatures allow particulates to settle less quickly |

*Wildfire Season Alert*: From late summer through fall, Southern California often experiences elevated PM₂.₅ concentrations because of regional fires. Even when the AQI looks “moderate,” fine particles may still pose risks for sensitive groups.

---

### Health Tips Based on AQI Levels

| AQI Category | Suggested Actions |
|--------------|------------------|
| Good (≤50) | Normal outdoor activities. No special precautions needed. |
| Moderate (51–100) | Light exercise okay. Those with asthma might notice mild symptoms. |
| Unhealthy for Sensitive Groups (101–150) | Reduce prolonged exertion outdoors. Keep windows closed. Consider wearing N95 respirators if you plan to stay outside long. |
| Unhealthy (151–200) | Avoid strenuous activity. Stay indoors with filtered air. Use HEPA filters or air purifiers. |
| Very Unhealthy/Hazardous (>200) | Limit time outside entirely. Seek indoor spaces with clean air. Monitor medical conditions closely. |

---

### Quick Reference Table (Example Values — Not Live Data)

| Date | City Center AQI | Main Pollutant | Comment |
|------|-----------------|----------------|---------|
| 2024‑04‑15 | 78 | Ozone | Mildly higher than usual due to sunny skies. |
| 2024‑07‑02 | 112 | PM₂.₅ | Wildfire haze present; moderate risk for asthmatics. |
| 2024‑09‑20 | 45 | Ozone | Excellent air quality after rain clearing dust. |

*(These numbers illustrate typical ranges; always verify against a live source.)*

---

### Bottom Line

To know **today’s exact AQI for Los Angeles**, head straight to **[AirNow](https://www.airnow.gov)** or another trusted platform listed above. Once you’ve got the figure, compare it to the categories above to decide whether you should adjust your plans or take protective measures.

If you’d like me to explain more about interpreting individual pollutant readings or setting up automated alerts, just let me know!
